title: Know Your No-Go’s for Hiring
author: Chris O'Brien
summary: Chris O'Brien, a school founder and principal, argues that hiring failures stem from never having decided in advance what you will not compromise on. He recounts three bad hires, one made on a résumé, one that overlooked ego, one that ignored how a candidate treated students, and concludes that charisma exploits any interviewer who has not written down standards beforehand. He names three traits he hires for (reflective, coachable, resilient) and two he refuses to coach (ego and blaming families). A story of instantly hiring a future principal on a university track field house shows the payoff of deciding first. His closing move reframes hiring as a designed system rather than an event, one that elicits behavior through tasks rather than rehearsed answers.
points: Bad hires share one root cause: the interviewer had not decided beforehand what was non-negotiable, so charisma filled the gap.
The author hires for reflective, coachable and resilient candidates, traits that can be developed but not installed from scratch.
Ego and blaming families are treated as values problems, not coaching problems, so they are screened out rather than trained away.
Hiring should be a designed process: tasks produce behavior, while questions merely produce rehearsed answers.
quotes: Charisma finds unprepared interviewers the way water finds cracks. Not maliciously. Just efficiently.
I had confused evidence of past performance with evidence of future fit — and those are not the same question.

Coachable. Feedback lands as information rather than judgment. They don’t defend. They don’t redirect. They get curious. You can actually test this in the interview itself — push back gently on something they say and watch what happens. That moment tells you more than the next three questions combined.
These traits can be developed over time. They cannot be installed from scratch. The candidate who arrives without them will consume more of your time and energy than they return.

I am not willing to coach ego out of someone. The candidate who enters with quiet superiority — who positions their experience as evidence of their ceiling rather than their floor, who bristles subtly when their ideas are challenged — that person will not thrive in a culture built on collective ownership. Ego is not a coaching problem. It’s a values problem. And values don’t change because feedback is skillfully delivered.

The difference between a screen that surfaces and a screen that performs is the difference between a question and a task. Questions produce answers. Tasks produce behavior. Behavior is what you’re actually hiring.

Write your non-negotiables down before the first candidate sits across from you. Put them somewhere you’ll see them before every interview. Not because you’ll forget them in the abstract — but because charisma is not abstract. It’s specific and present and sitting right across from you, and it will talk you out of your standards every time if you haven’t already decided they aren’t negotiable.
